# Preface {.unnumbered}

Machine learning systems usually end at an output. A classifier returns a
label. A language model returns text. The software around them can be complex,
but the inference itself does not move the world.

**Physical AI** begins when that endpoint moves. The system's output becomes a
proposal for action. If the action is allowed, it changes the world that will
produce the next observation. The system then lives with its own consequences.

That change reorganizes the engineering problem. Observations age. Belief is
never free. A capable proposal can still be late, stale, or unsafe. Someone—or
some independent path—must decide what may reach actuators. Evidence gathered
offline can stop being valid once the system acts.

The durable question of this book is not which model is strongest. It is:

> What must the system know, measure, enforce, preserve, and prove before a
> learned proposal may produce a physical consequence?

## What Physical AI Systems Means Here

**Physical AI Systems** is the field and course name: systems engineering for
learned components that sense and act under constraint.

A system is in scope only when three conditions hold:

1. a **learned component** materially influences the action path;
2. an allowed action produces **consequential physical feedback**—it changes
   task-relevant world state and can alter later observations or choices; and
3. the system holds **delegated physical authority** over that action
   (permission to move, not only to advise).

Placing a model on a robot is not enough. An advisory display with sensors is
not enough. Closing the loop with authority over matter is what forces the rest
of the book.

## TinyAgents Kit

The laboratory companion is the **TinyAgents Kit**: a dual-brain educational
platform on Arduino UNO Q (Linux MPU + real-time MCU).

| Term | Meaning in this book |
| --- | --- |
| **TinyAgent** | A complete engineered agent under resource and physical limits: sense, represent, estimate, propose, permit, act, measure, and respect human authority |
| **Not** | A chat loop, an unconstrained tool-using LLM, or “TinyML plus a large model” |
| **TinyML** | Deploy a model under tight compute |
| **TinyAgents** | Build an intelligent machine whose proposals still need permission to move |

> TinyML taught you to deploy a model. TinyAgents teaches you to build an
> intelligent machine.

On the kit, that permission is *made physical*:

| Brain | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **MPU** (rich, best-effort) | Perception, state, policies, planning, tools, logs—**proposes** |
| **MCU** (trusted real-time) | Timing-critical loops, watchdogs, limits, validation, safe fallback—**permits** |
| **Boundary** | Typed, timestamped, **expiring intent**; the MCU may permit, refuse, interrupt, or recover |

The dual-brain split is a teaching realization of proposal versus permission
(runtime-assurance lineage). It is not a claim of industrial functional-safety
certification. Concepts in the book stay platform-neutral; the kit is the
reference body for the labs.

## How the Book Relates to the Course

**Physical AI Systems** is one open project-based course: enrolled cohorts and
anyone following along (including kit partners) use the same schedule,
milestones, design dossier, and TinyAgents Kit path. The book is the method
library for that course—not a separate curriculum product.

Three teaching blocks, then a capstone:

| Block | Chapters | Job |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| **I. Foundations** | 1–4 | Scope, world requirements, metrology, continuous dual-brain runtime |
| **II. Building a TinyAgent** | 5–10 | Observe → estimate → propose → permit → place → qualify |
| **III. Responsibility** | 11–13 | Authority, governed learning, deploy / condition / refuse |
| **Capstone** | Final review | Transfer and diagnosed failure—no new theory |

Each chapter completes one capability, one decision, and one dossier piece.
Primitives to click together: **loop, time, budget, permission, evidence**.

## How Chapters and Labs Relate

Every chapter is conceptually complete before hardware. Labs do not invent
theory. The course project integrates kit experiences rather than assigning
thirteen peer-weight kit nights. Analytical and hosted substitutes remain valid
for the same decision.

## The Standard

The book succeeds if a graduate meets an unfamiliar embodiment and model and
asks better questions than “Which model should I run?”

What is the causal boundary? How old is the belief when action takes effect?
What may the model only propose? What may refuse it? What continues when the
policy is late? What does the evidence actually prove? Who may teach, stop,
revoke, and forget? What would justify—or refuse—deployment?

Models and boards will change. Those questions should not.
